The Morality of Meat

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We ask whether the time has come for all of us to give up eating meat to help save the planet.

Unique Selling Point:
It's estimated that animal agriculture accounts for around 14% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Protests, increasingly frequent and vocal, are now targeting the sector as vociferously as the fossil fuel industry as they call for greater action on climate change. We take to the streets of London to hear from vegan protesters who've joined ranks with the Extinction Rebellion movement to have their voices heard. We also travel to rural Wales to hear the thoughts of a dairy farmer who feels the sector is misunderstood and - often - unfairly targeted.

Summary:
This insert will examine one of the clarion calls of the global movement calling for stronger action to halt climate change: that, in order to reduce the levels of greenhouse gasses in our atmosphere, we need to stop eating meat. Granted, not all climate change activists are vegan but it's a lifestyle of world view with increasing influence. Whats-more, far from being easily-dismissed as the rantings of a group of hemp-wearing tree-huggers, they appear to have science on their side. Not only does animal agriculture contribute to mass deforestation and water consumption, but it's claimed it's directly responsible for a significant amount of methane and carbon di-oxide pollution. The vegan perspective is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore; and that's without even considering their arguments in favour of animal welfare.

At the same time, the meat and dairy sectors, are fighting their corner. "Yes, there are rogue elements", they say. "But ours is an industry falsely accused of mistreating animals and being unwilling to become more sustainable". One such person is Abi Reader, a dairy farmer in Wales. In response to the onslaught, she is proactively marketing the dairy industry, the good that it does, and the relationship many farmers have with their herd. She's not afraid of controversy and speaks out strongly again militant veganism, an off-shoot of the movement we'll also dwell on in the insert.

Along the way, we'll examine the science and ask whether ending meat production will have the impact vegans argue it will, or whether their voices are drowning out more meaningful discussions on the fossil fuel industry.

Press Release:


Could the End of Meat Save the Planet?
Is it time to stop eating meat to help save the planet? Well that’s the line of argument that some climate change activists are pushing in a bid to pull the earth back from the brink. To feed the world’s meat addiction, animal agriculture contributes to deforestation, as well as methane and carbon di-oxide pollution. Now in the United Kingdom, vegan protesters have joined the ranks of the Extinction Rebellion movement, to demand that government takes action to avoid a climate tipping point. But meat and dairy producers are fighting back. So could radical lifestyle changes really make a difference? Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: John Webb | Presenter: John Webb


Script:


VO: It resembled a mass celebration; a carnival of music and dance on the streets of central London. But, the chanting and songs of protest hinted at something far more significant.

(Pause)

VO: The protestors arrived in early October, united in their call for action on climate change. They had answered the call of an organisation that – a little more than 12 months ago - nobody had heard of.

Link Extinction Rebellion: In just over a year the Extinction Rebellion Movement has exploded into something that can do this: bring significant parts of a city like London to a standstill. It believes in peaceful civil disobedience under the motto “Rebel for Life”

VO: It’s now a worldwide movement; home to people concerned about global warming and the environment. People like Darcy Mitchell

Darcy Mitchell [03:01:49] STRAP “Extinction Rebellion, Bristol” I've got my son here with me and tell him everything's going to be all right but there's actually no point doing that unless you're going to speak up for them and make sure that this very, very real threat gets dealt with.

Link Extinction Rebellion 2: It would be easy to dismiss the yoga, pithy banners and occasional pink Octopus as a fad. But this is an organisation that wants to be heard and is being heard.

VO: That might be down to just how relentless these protests are – this one isn’t the first and it certainly won’t be the last.

Alex Lockwood [02:02:57] it's been an incredible, incredibly uplifting and empowering experience so far. I think we've reached a lot of people. We've got our message heard. And we're really hoping that actually the government's going to listen.

VO: But Alex Lockwood’s message is more complex than it might appear. Yes, he’s concerned about climate change, but he’s primarily here for the animals. He’s the spokesperson for Animal Rebellion, a sort of movement within a movement.

Alex Lockwood [02:05:23] STRAP “Spokesperson: Animal Rebellion” One of the things we wanted to do was make sure that the animal voice wasn't lost in the climate message even though the climate message is really pressing and it is urgent.

VO: These days, though, it’s hard to separate the animal voice from concerns around climate change – the two have become inseparable. “Express concern around the environment but continue eating meat”, these demonstrators say, “and you’re a hypocrite”.

Alex Lockwood [02:04:22] The food system on which we rely, which really is broken and so that we need to fix it and the best way to fix that is transition to a plant-based food system.

VO: And, for Lockwood and his compatriots, what is most in need of “fixing” is this: what’s referred to as animal agriculture. To meet the food demands of a growing global population – the majority of whom are meat and dairy eaters – it often operates on an industrial scale. So, when it comes to veganism and its ties to the climate change campaign, we’re talking about quite specific animals – how they’re treated, why they’re consumed and, crucially, the environmental cost of both.

VO: The most credible studies put meat and dairy’s contribution to human-caused global greenhouse gas emissions at between 13 and 18%. That’s less than fossil fuel combustion for energy and transport, but still significant.

(Pause)

VO: They also use about 70 percent of agricultural land, and, according to some estimates, producing a serving of beef emits 316 times more greenhouse gas than a serving of lentils or beans. Often criticised as overly simplistic, they’re estimates embraced by the vegan community.

Toni Brockhoven [19:47:26] We don't argue with the science. We have no reason to doubt it. And in fact, as far back as 2010, the United Nations actually stated that the most urgent way of combating climate change is to reduce or eliminate our dependence on animal agriculture.

VO: Toni Brockhoven is the chair of Beauty Without Cruelty, and an organiser of animal rights protests here in South Africa.

Toni Brockhoven [19:51:41] We are in trouble and we are causing it and we need to make changes. And one of those changes is eliminating animal products as far as possible from our lives

VO: According to some surveys the number of vegans in the UK has quadrupled to 600 thousand in the past five years. There aren’t exact figures, but there’s likely to have been growth in South Africa, too. If the London protests are anything to go by, at least part of that is being driven by concern about the impact of climate change.

Toni Brockhoven [20:01:28]: It is quite true that you cannot be a true environmentalist and continue to consume animals in the same way that you can't call yourself an animal lover and consume them. You can be a pet lover. You can be a wildlife lover. You can be a marine animal lover. But you can't do both.

VO: That’s long been the view of vegans, but it has different context now: it’s no longer purely about animal welfare, they say, but about potentially catastrophic changes to our planet.

(Pause)

VO: It’s also a view strongly disputed in the places where providing food shapes a way of life. Places like rural Wales - which seems both busy and serene at the same time. Farming country.

(Pause)

VO: This is home to 180 cows, several calves, and a dairy farmed called Abi Reader. Sometimes, you meet people you can’t imagine doing anything else. She’s one of them.

Abi Reader [00:00:06] I'm a third-generation farmer. My grandfather got married and moved here back in the 30s. I was born here on the farm.

VO: As connected to this land as her family is, so too are her cows.

Abi Reader [00:00:32] STRAP “Dairy Farmer” When he moved here in the thirties, when he got married, he bought some cows with him (CUT) and started up the farm here. So all of the cows here are descended from those would have been about five or six cows.

VO: It’s the ideal existence for someone historically and emotionally attached to this land. But it’s an increasingly uneasy one.

Link Farm: Rural Wales is a long way from the hustle and bustle of central London. But, in many ways, this is what the fight is all about. It might not look it, but this is a climate change frontline.

VO: Not quite farming on an industrial scale, but a target of the vegan climate change lobby, none-the-less.

Abi Reader [00:02:07] it's very frustrating when you are, you know, I'm part of a system that produces food for this country. (CUT) And then when people criticize it, it really does grind quite a lot (CUT) [00:03:29] It's all very well to have this idealistic view of food produced on a little allotment and it can feed you for a year. It can't. It needs farms like mine to be able to do that.

VO: Reader’s increasingly having to fight her corner; her cows no longer purely producers of milk, cheese and butter but a focal point in the battle against climate change.

(Pause)

VO: Her cause isn’t being helped by the growing body of research on the subject – studies like the one conducted by America’s Johns Hopkins University just a few months ago. It concluded that, if we all turned vegan, food-related carbon emissions would be cut by 70%. While the vegan movement continues to pursue that outcome, it also found a diet free of dairy would cut those emissions by 23%.

John Question: Are you concerned about your industry?

Abi Reader[00:12:10] It's certainly putting a lot of pressure on now. If you'd asked me that question a year ago, I would have said, no, I'm not concerned. I think, you know, I'm going to have to revise that opinion.

VO: And that pressure has come despite the impact of animal agriculture on climate being hotly contested: the numbers change, for example, depending on where a product is farmed and whether it’s consumed locally or exported. It’s also pressure, says Reader, that ignores the consequences of turning against meat and dairy.

Abi Reader [00:12:52] If we lost livestock here in Wales, it would be absolutely devastating for the majority of Wales. 80 percent of the land area here in Wales is farmed. And a lot of those areas support rural communities which again preserve our culture our heritage, particularly our Welsh language. That would probably disappear.

VO: For those calling for change, including the vegan movement helping to drive the climate change agenda, our options are fast running out.

Toni Brockhoven [19:54:34] one of the tenets is that we need to reduce or eliminate animal use completely. I don't think it's unrealistic. I think it's going to be very difficult because we have personal choice and we have culture and we have religion and we have we've always done it this way. But it's really quite simple. What side of history do you want to be on?

Alex Lockwood [02:10:00] change only happens in a crisis and our job is to make sure that the ideas are on the table when that crisis hits (CUT) and the climate change is bringing a crisis, then the ideas that are closest to hand will be the ones that people implement.

VO: Reader, though, has other ideas.

John Question: Do you think you’ll still be farming here in 15, 20 years?

Abi Reader [00:15:32] Yeah, I'll be here. May look a little bit different, but I'll be here and my cows will too.

Ends…

metadata.Summary: This insert will examine one of the clarion calls of the global movement calling for stronger action to halt climate change: that, in order to reduce the levels of greenhouse gasses in our atmosphere, we need to stop eating meat. Granted, not all climate change activists are vegan but it's a lifestyle of world view with increasing influence. Whats-more, far from being easily-dismissed as the rantings of a group of hemp-wearing tree-huggers, they appear to have science on their side. Not only does animal agriculture contribute to mass deforestation and water consumption, but it's claimed it's directly responsible for a significant amount of methane and carbon di-oxide pollution. The vegan perspective is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore; and that's without even considering their arguments in favour of animal welfare. At the same time, the meat and dairy sectors, are fighting their corner. "Yes, there are rogue elements", they say. "But ours is an industry falsely accused of mistreating animals and being unwilling to become more sustainable". One such person is Abi Reader, a dairy farmer in Wales. In response to the onslaught, she is proactively marketing the dairy industry, the good that it does, and the relationship many farmers have with their herd. She's not afraid of controversy and speaks out strongly again militant veganism, an off-shoot of the movement we'll also dwell on in the insert. Along the way, we'll examine the science and ask whether ending meat production will have the impact vegans argue it will, or whether their voices are drowning out more meaningful discussions on the fossil fuel industry.
